claims.claim: UPF1 was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression.
claims.source: UPF1 (UP-Frameshift-1) is a universally conserved eukaryotic protein that was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression (Culbertson et al., 1980; Leeds et al., 1992), and gained other names – including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) – from other genetic screens (Altamura et al., 1992; Hodgkin et al., 1989; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the original genetic screen publications.

claims.claim: UPF1 gained other names including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) from other genetic screens.
claims.source: UPF1 (UP-Frameshift-1) is a universally conserved eukaryotic protein that was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression (Culbertson et al., 1980; Leeds et al., 1992), and gained other names – including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) – from other genetic screens (Altamura et al., 1992; Hodgkin et al., 1989; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the relevant genetic screen publications.

claims.claim: Cells that lack active UPF1 accumulate mRNAs with nonsense, frameshift or other mutant alleles that introduce a premature translation termination codon (PTC).
claims.source: Cells that lack active UPF1 accumulate mRNAs with nonsense, frameshift or other mutant alleles that introduce a premature translation termination codon (PTC) (Leeds et al., 1991; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this phenotype.

claims.claim: UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
claims.source: These observations are generally interpreted as evidence that UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely (Fatscher et al., 2015; He and Jacobson, 2015; Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
claims.evidence: This represents the general interpretation in the field, supported by multiple review citations.

claims.claim: NMD is a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely.
claims.source: These observations are generally interpreted as evidence that UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely (Fatscher et al., 2015; He and Jacobson, 2015; Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple review citations.

claims.claim: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins.
claims.source: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins and that regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation (Goetz and Wilkinson, 2017; Lykke-Andersen and Jensen, 2015).
claims.evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field, supported by review citations.

claims.claim: NMD regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation.
claims.source: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins and that regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation (Goetz and Wilkinson, 2017; Lykke-Andersen and Jensen, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by review citations discussing the regulatory roles of NMD.

claims.claim: Standard models postulate that UPF1 monitors translation termination on ribosomes by interacting with a peptide release factor (eRF1 or eRF3).
claims.source: Standard models postulate that UPF1 monitors translation termination on ribosomes by interacting with a peptide release factor (eRF1 or eRF3).
claims.evidence: This represents the standard model in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'standard models postulate'.

claims.claim: Recent reports on mammalian translation systems have suggested that UPF1 does not bind to either eRF1 or eRF3, in contrast to earlier reports on other organisms.
claims.source: However, recent reports on mammalian translation systems have suggested, in contrast to earlier reports on other organisms (Czaplinski et al., 1998; Ivanov et al., 2008; Kashima et al., 2006; Keeling et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2001), that UPF1 does not bind to either of these.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to both recent and earlier conflicting reports.

claims.claim: Recent reports suggested that UPF3B may contact release factors, slow the termination of translation and facilitate post-termination release of ribosomes.
claims.source: They suggested, instead, that UPF3B may contact release factors, slow the termination of translation and facilitate post-termination release of ribosomes – and so fulfil the termination monitoring role that has been assigned to UPF1 (Neu-Yilik et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures.
claims.source: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures and so can displace RNA-bound proteins (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Czaplinski et al., 1995; Fiorini et al., 2015; Franks et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical studies.

claims.claim: UPF1 can displace RNA-bound proteins.
claims.source: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures and so can displace RNA-bound proteins (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Czaplinski et al., 1995; Fiorini et al., 2015; Franks et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical studies.

claims.claim: UPF1 is predominantly associated with 3'UTRs of cytoplasmic mRNAs.
claims.source: UPF1 is predominantly associated with 3'UTRs of cytoplasmic mRNAs which indicates that it might be selectively recruited to or activated on NMD targets with abnormally long 3'UTRs (Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing this association pattern.

claims.claim: UPF1 appears to bind mRNAs fairly indiscriminately, regardless of the position of the stop codon or the PTC.
claims.source: However, UPF1 appears to bind mRNAs fairly indiscriminately, regardless of the position of the stop codon or the PTC and whether or not the mRNA possess NMD-inducing features such as an abnormally long 3'UTR or an exon junction downstream of the stop codon (Hogg and Goff, 2010; Hurt et al., 2013; Zünd et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing broad UPF1 binding patterns.

claims.claim: UPF1 helicase activity is required for NMD.
claims.source: UPF1 helicase activity is required for NMD, but how it helps to target particular transcripts for NMD remains unclear.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: It has been questioned whether cells do possess any mechanism to discriminate between PTCs and normal stop codons.
claims.source: In view of these and other perplexing observations, it has also been questioned whether cells do possess any such mechanism to discriminate between PTCs and normal stop codons (Brogna et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review questioning this mechanism.

claims.claim: UPF1 is most abundant in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: UPF1 is most abundant in the cytoplasm where its roles discussed above depend on ribosomal translation and occur on cytoplasmic mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation data (Figure 1C) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: A fraction of UPF1 was expected in the nucleus, as the protein traffics in and out of the nucleus in mammalian cells.
claims.source: A fraction of UPF1 was expected in the nucleus though, as the protein traffics in and out of the nucleus in mammalian cells (Ajamian et al., 2015; Mendell et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in mammalian cells.

claims.claim: Some studies have concluded that within the nucleus UPF1 plays a distinct and direct role in DNA replication.
claims.source: Some studies have concluded that within the nucleus UPF1 plays a distinct and direct role in DNA replication, which would be unrelated to gene expression (Azzalin and Lingner, 2006; Azzalin et al., 2007; Carastro et al., 2002; Chawla et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing this role.

claims.claim: The negative effects that depletion of UPF1 has on DNA replication and cell division could be an indirect consequence of NMD suppression altering the expression of genes required in such processes.
claims.source: However, the negative effects that depletion of UPF1 has on DNA replication and cell division could be an indirect consequence of NMD suppression altering the expression of genes required in such processes (Varsally and Brogna, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an alternative interpretation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: There is evidence that nuclear UPF1 might contribute directly to RNA processing, at least in specific instances.
claims.source: Moreover, there is evidence that nuclear UPF1 might contribute directly to RNA processing, at least in specific instances, and is required for nuclear export of HIV-1 genomic RNA in HeLa cells (Ajamian et al., 2015; de Turris et al., 2011; Flury et al., 2014; Varsally and Brogna, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing these roles.

claims.claim: UPF1 is required for nuclear export of HIV-1 genomic RNA in HeLa cells.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study in HeLa cells.

claims.claim: CLIP data indicate direct binding of UPF1 with the abundant nuclear-localised metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (MALAT1) in mammalian cells.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to CLIP data.

claims.claim: Three monoclonal anti-peptide antibodies were generated that target regions of Drosophila UPF1 outside the RNA helicase domain.
claims.source: To explore the functions of UPF1, we generated three monoclonal anti-peptide antibodies that target regions of Drosophila UPF1 outside the RNA helicase domain: one epitope in the N-terminal flanking regions (antibody 1C13 against Pep2), and two near the C-terminus (Ab 7D17 vs. Pep11; and Ab 7B12 vs. Pep12) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 1).

claims.claim: Each antibody detected UPF1 as a single band by western blotting of Drosophila S2 cell extracts, with minimal cross-reactivity to other proteins.

claims.claim: The antibodies detected a second, larger band of the expected molecular weight in extracts from transfected S2 cells that over-express UPF1-GFP.

claims.claim: UPF1-RNAi specifically reduced the amount of UPF1 in S2 cells without affecting the levels of several other proteins tested as controls.

claims.claim: Following cell fractionation of S2 cells, a small proportion of the UPF1 co-purified with nuclei whilst most was in the cytoplasmic fraction.
claims.source: Following cell fractionation of S2 cells, α-tubulin and RNA Pol II were, as expected, restricted to the cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, respectively – and a small proportion of the UPF1 co-purified with nuclei whilst most was in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 1C), consistent with the subcellular localisation detected by immunostaining.

claims.claim: UPF1 was most abundant in the cytoplasm and perinuclear region in Drosophila salivary glands, with distinct but less intense nuclear staining.
claims.source: UPF1 was most abundant in the cytoplasm and perinuclear region, and there was also distinct but less intense nuclear staining, mainly around the chromosomes and around the nucleolus (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: A similar subcellular distribution of UPF1 was detected with the remaining two antibodies tested in wild-type salivary glands.

claims.claim: The UPF1 signal was drastically reduced in UPF1-RNAi glands, consistent with all three antibodies being specific.

claims.claim: UPF1 was detected both in the cytoplasm and in the nucleus in other larval tissues, with varying immunostaining intensities.

claims.claim: In enterocytes (EC), UPF1 staining was similar between the cytoplasm and the nucleus, while the most intense UPF1 signal was perinuclear.

claims.claim: WGA is a lectin that predominantly interacts with O-GlcNAc-modified nuclear pore proteins.

claims.claim: Almost all of the UPF1 in each cell compartment was rapidly mobile, with the halftime for repopulation of each bleached area being only a few seconds.

claims.claim: Actin5C displayed one of the brightest UPF1 chromosomal signals at the gene locus corresponding to interband 5C on the X chromosome.

claims.claim: UPF1 enrichment was greatest at highly expressed genes.

claims.claim: A close correlation was observed between UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II ChIP-seq signals.

claims.claim: A close correlation was observed between UPF1-ChIP signals and mRNA levels.

claims.claim: UPF1 is associated with genes throughout their transcription units, particularly with highly expressed genes.

claims.claim: Ser2 Pol II typically shows higher loading around transcription start sites (TSS) corresponding to promoter-proximal Pol II pausing sites.

claims.claim: Most gene-associated UPF1 was further downstream than the TSS-proximal Ser2 Pol II peak, especially at highly expressed genes.

claims.claim: UPF1 did not associate with genes at which Ser2 Pol II was associated only with the TSS pausing site and which were not being actively transcribed.

claims.claim: The association of UPF1 with Pol II transcription sites is partially sensitive to RNase treatment.

claims.claim: UPF1 association was less sensitive to RNase treatment than that of the RNA binding protein hnRNPA1.
claims.source: UPF1 association was, though, less sensitive to RNase treatment than that of the RNA binding protein hnRNPA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), which is almost completely detached from the chromosome following the same RNase treatment.

claims.claim: Some of UPF1 co-purifies with Ser2 Pol II in a standard immunoprecipitation of S2 nuclear cell extracts, the interaction being sensitive to RNase treatment.

claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: DRB markedly reduced the amount of UPF1 associated with gene loci in salivary glands.
claims.source: DRB treatment, as expected, left interbands and puffs cytologically unaffected, however, it markedly reduced the amount of UPF1 associated with gene loci (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E), providing further evidence that transcript elongation into the body of the gene is needed for this association to occur.

claims.claim: DRB reduced the association of UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II with genes in S2 cells.
claims.source: DRB also reduced the association of UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II with genes, such as the highly expressed RpL23A, in S2 cells (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data comparing control and DRB-treated cells.

claims.claim: UPF1 binds at some Pol III genes including 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs.
claims.source: UPF1 was found mainly at Pol II transcription sites, most of which are protein-coding genes, however, our ChIP-seq data revealed that UPF1 also binds at some Pol III genes. The latter included 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) – but not, for example, the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: UPF1 does not bind to the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes.
claims.source: UPF1 was found mainly at Pol II transcription sites, most of which are protein-coding genes, however, our ChIP-seq data revealed that UPF1 also binds at some Pol III genes. The latter included 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) – but not, for example, the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data showing no UPF1 signal at tRNA genes.

claims.claim: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription.
claims.source: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and see also the earlier discussion of heat-shock gene activation), so recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data and heat-shock experiments.

claims.claim: UPF1 recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
claims.source: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and see also the earlier discussion of heat-shock gene activation), so recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UPF1 associates with both intron-containing and intronless genes.

claims.claim: Within intron-containing genes, more UPF1 was associated with exons than with introns.
claims.source: Within intron-containing genes, however, more UPF1 was associated with exons than with introns – as can be seen in the ChIP-seq profiles of highly UPF1-enriched genes such as Xrp1 (Figure 5A; and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows other examples of genes displaying this pattern).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A and related figures.

claims.claim: Relatively more of UPF1 is associated with downstream exons than with the first exon at several genes.
claims.source: Additionally, it appears that relatively more of UPF1 is associated with downstream exons than with the first exon, at Xrp1 as well as several of the other genes; notably, in many such cases most of the first exon corresponds to the 5'UTR (see examples in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments.
claims.source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The exon-biased UPF1 enrichment is genome-wide.
claims.source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left flanking exon (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (p=2.391e-9) compared to introns.
claims.source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The normal bias towards UPF1-exon association in Xrp1 was abolished in U1-70K-depleted cells.

claims.claim: The bias towards UPF1-exon association persisted in cells depleted of eIF4AIII or Y14.

claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Y14 and eIF4III are two EJC proteins that bind the nascent pre-mRNA but are not likely to play a direct splicing role in Drosophila.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced.
claims.source: Moreover, genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as Xrp1, are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced (see the Nascent RNA-seq profile in Figure 5A), whereas genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as CG5059, are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and are typically expressed at low levels, as reported (Khodor et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced and are typically expressed at low levels.
claims.source: Moreover, genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as Xrp1, are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced (see the Nascent RNA-seq profile in Figure 5A), whereas genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as CG5059, are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and are typically expressed at low levels, as reported (Khodor et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by nascent RNA-seq data and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Intron recognition interferes with the association of UPF1 with the unspliced nascent transcript.
claims.source: It seems therefore, that intron recognition interferes with the association of UPF1 with the unspliced nascent transcript.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing exon-biased UPF1 enrichment and its dependence on U1 snRNP.

claims.claim: In wild-type cells poly(A) was abundant and fairly evenly distributed throughout the cytoplasm, with relatively little in the nuclei.
claims.source: In wild-type cells poly(A) was abundant and fairly evenly distributed throughout the cytoplasm, as would be expected for mature mRNA, and there was relatively little in the nuclei (Figure 6A, panels I-III).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The nuclei of UPF1-depleted cells retained a substantial amount of poly(A), and the cells appeared to contain less cytoplasmic poly(A) than wild-type cells.
claims.source: By contrast, the nuclei of UPF1-depleted cells retained a substantial amount of poly(A), and the cells appeared to contain less cytoplasmic poly(A) than wild-type cells (Figure 6A, panels IV-VI).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data comparing wild-type and UPF1-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Much of the nuclear-retained poly(A) in the UPF1-depleted cells formed large cluster(s) in either inter-chromosomal spaces or in surrounding nucleoli.
claims.source: Much of the nuclear-retained poly(A) in the UPF1-depleted cells formed large cluster(s) in either inter-chromosomal spaces (Figure 6A, panel VI, white arrow) or, possibly more frequently, in surrounding nucleoli (yellow arrow) that seemed neither linked to or in the proximity of any specific chromosomal region(s) or defined transcription site(s).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no nuclear poly(A) accumulation.
claims.source: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no such nuclear poly(A) accumulation (Figure 6A, panels VII-IX); indicating that this phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data in UPF1-RNAi cells expressing human UPF1.

claims.claim: The nuclear poly(A) accumulation phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
claims.source: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no such nuclear poly(A) accumulation (Figure 6A, panels VII-IX); indicating that this phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that human UPF1 expression prevents poly(A) accumulation.

claims.claim: No poly(A) accumulation was observed in UPF31 mutant glands, or following RNAi depletion of the EJC components Y14 or MAGO.
claims.source: Additionally, no poly(A) accumulation was observed in UPF31 mutant glands, or following RNAi depletion of the EJC components Y14 or MAGO (unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claims.claim: Expression of hUPF1 suppressed the apparent smaller size of the salivary glands depleted of the endogenous UPF1.
claims.source: Expression of hUPF1 also suppressed the apparent smaller size of the salivary glands depleted of the endogenous UPF1; these glands were comparable in size to that of wild-type (Figure 6A, panels I and VII vs IV).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing gland sizes in the images shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes.
claims.source: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes. However, a few interbands – such as 2C at the distal end of the X chromosome (Figure 6B) – showed clear poly(A) signals (Figure 6B, left panel), suggesting that some mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated remain associated, at least briefly, with some transcription sites.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A few interbands such as 2C showed clear poly(A) signals in wild-type chromosomes, suggesting that some mature mRNAs remain associated with some transcription sites.
claims.source: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes. However, a few interbands – such as 2C at the distal end of the X chromosome (Figure 6B) – showed clear poly(A) signals (Figure 6B, left panel), suggesting that some mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated remain associated, at least briefly, with some transcription sites.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data and the authors' interpretation.

claims.claim: The poly(A) accumulation at 2C in wild-type cells may be a consequence of lack of UPF1 at this transcription site.
claims.source: Additionally, since UPF1 was obviously not associated with 2C (see Figure 3A), the poly(A) accumulation at 2C in wild-type cells may be a consequence of lack of UPF1 at this transcription site.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that 2C shows poly(A) accumulation but no UPF1 association.

claims.claim: Both the number of transcriptional sites showing poly(A) accumulation and the amount of poly(A) RNA associated with these sites were strikingly increased in UPF1-depleted cells.
claims.source: Both the number of transcriptional sites showing poly(A) accumulation and the amount of poly(A) RNA associated with these sites were strikingly increased in UPF1-depleted cells (Figure 6B, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes comparing wild-type and UPF1-depleted cells.

claims.claim: There was no visible poly(A) accumulation at site 5C (Actin5C gene) in wild-type, but this band was obviously fluorescent in UPF1-depleted cells.
claims.source: For example, there was no visible poly(A) accumulation at site 5C, which corresponds to the highly transcribed Actin5C gene, in wild-type, but this band was obviously fluorescent in UPF1-depleted cells.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Site 2B showed a faint poly(A) signal in wild-type glands and a strong signal in UPF1-depleted cells.
claims.source: Another example was site 2B – where constitutively expressed sta and rush are probably the most active genes at this larval stage – which showed a faint poly(A) signal in wild-type glands and a strong signal in UPF1-depleted cells.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: UPF1 was clearly associated with transcription sites 2B and 5C on polytene chromosomes and in S2 cells.
claims.source: UPF1 was clearly associated with these transcription sites (2B and 5C) on polytene chromosomes (Figure 3A) and in S2 cells (as detected by ChIP: see Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for the UPF1 profile of Actin5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: UPF1 plays important role(s) in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and in their transport out of the nucleus.
claims.source: Cumulatively, the data indicate that UPF1 plays important role(s) in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and in their transport out of the nucleus (Figure 6C shows a cartoon of a transcription site in either a wild-type or UPF1 depleted cell with or without mRNA retention).
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the cumulative data showing poly(A) retention in UPF1-depleted cells.

claims.claim: UPF1 shuttling depends on the ATPase activity of the RNA helicase domain, which is required for the dynamic binding and dissociation of UPF1 from mRNAs in both yeast and mammalian cells.
claims.source: In contrast, we present evidence that UPF1 moves constantly within and between cell compartments, and that this shuttling depends on the ATPase activity of the RNA helicase domain, which is required for the dynamic binding and dissociation of UPF1 from mRNAs in both yeast and mammalian cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and citations to studies in yeast and mammalian cells.

claims.claim: UPF1 ATPase domain resides within a region previously thought to contain an atypical nuclear localisation signal in mammalian cells.
claims.source: Notably, UPF1 ATPase domain resides within a region previously thought to contain an atypical nuclear localisation signal in mammalian cells, which when deleted, abolished nuclear UPF1 accumulation following LMB treatment (Mendell et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study in mammalian cells.

claims.claim: Typical UPF1 subcellular distribution is primarily a consequence of its continued association with abundant RNA cargos that are being continuously exported out of the nucleus.
claims.source: However, in view of UPF1 ATPase activity being required for this shuttling, we propose that typical UPF1 subcellular distribution, with more of the protein present in the cytoplasm than in the nucleus, is primarily a consequence of its continued association with abundant RNA cargos that are being continuously exported out of the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of their data.

claims.claim: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms.
claims.source: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms (Herold et al., 2003; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007), yet it is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP) (Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The CRM1 export pathway is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP).
claims.source: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms (Herold et al., 2003; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007), yet it is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP) (Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA.
claims.source: Our data indicate that UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which make the SRP scaffold.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq data showing UPF1 association with 7SL RNA genes.

claims.claim: 7SL RNA makes the SRP scaffold.
claims.source: Our data indicate that UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which make the SRP scaffold.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about SRP structure.

claims.claim: UPF1 may not be binding the individual 40S and 60S subunits, as less UPF1 is detected in the centre of the nucleolus than in the remainder of the nucleus.
claims.source: However, UPF1 may not be binding the individual 40S and 60S subunits, as less UPF1 is detected in the centre of the nucleolus than in the remainder of the nucleus - discussed further below.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing UPF1 exclusion from the nucleolus center.

claims.claim: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons.
claims.source: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Model 1), however, since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is one of two models proposed by the authors to explain the data.

claims.claim: Since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
claims.source: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Model 1), however, since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UPF1 associates with intronless genes.

claims.claim: UPF1 associates with all Pol II nascent transcripts, but on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, splice site recognition interferes with intron binding.
claims.source: Possibly, UPF1 associates with all Pol II nascent transcripts, but on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, splice site recognition interferes with intron binding.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of their data.

claims.claim: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly.
claims.source: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may therefore influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly; changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells (Brooks et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the authors' data and supported by a citation to a study showing splicing changes in UPF1-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells.
claims.source: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may therefore influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly; changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells (Brooks et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Simple affinity of UPF1 for RNA is not likely to be the primary reason why UPF1 associates with some nascent transcripts.
claims.source: Simple affinity of UPF1 for RNA is not likely to be the primary reason why UPF1 associates with some nascent transcripts, for several reasons: UPF1 does not associate with some highly transcribed Pol II genes, such as spliceosomal snRNAs; nor with snRNA U6 or other highly active Pol III genes; nor with rRNA genes transcribed by Pol I; there would be no differential affinity for introns vs. exons within a transcript; and UPF1 appears to be excluded from the RNA-packed centre of the nucleolus where rRNA genes are transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled (McLeod et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on multiple observations from their data.

claims.claim: One possible candidate feature that dictates UPF1 association would be the 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is added co-transcriptionally to the 5'end of pre-mRNAs but not to Pol I and Pol III transcripts.
claims.source: What features of some nascent transcripts, most often of Pol II-transcribed genes, dictate that UPF1 becomes associated with them remain to be determined. One possible candidate would be the 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is added co-transcriptionally to the 5'end of pre-mRNAs but not to Pol I and Pol III transcripts (Ghosh and Lima, 2010).

claims.claim: The m7G caps added to snRNAs and other small non-mRNA Pol II transcripts are further modified by hypermethylation to generate 2,2,7-trimethylguanosine(m(3)G) structures.
claims.source: Moreover, the m7G caps added to snRNAs and other small non-mRNA Pol II transcripts are further modified though by hypermethylation to generate 2,2,7-trimethylguanosine(m(3)G) structures (Mouaikel et al., 2002).

claims.source: Although this hypermethylation occurs after the transcripts have been exported to the cytoplasm in mammalian cells, perhaps this modification may occur in the nucleus instead in other organisms (Mouaikel et al., 2002), and this might explain why these classes of transcripts are not associated with UPF1 in Drosophila.

claims.claim: The association of UPF1 with nascent transcripts seems to be dynamic.

claims.evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP/FLIP data and the exon-biased enrichment pattern.

claims.source: In vitro, UPF1 can translocate along RNAs over long distances – but only at a maximum scanning velocity of ~80 base/min (Fiorini et al., 2015), which is much slower than the 2–3 kb/min of Pol II (Fiorini et al., 2015; Fukaya et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.source: Although this machinery is unlikely to be the Pol II itself, as we found no evidence of a strong direct association of Pol II with UPF1.

claims.claim: 5'UTRs are defined by the process of translation initiation, in which the 40S migrates downstream until it recognises the start codon.
claims.source: 5'UTRs are defined by the process of translation initiation, in which, following association with the mRNA's 5' cap, the 40S (carrying the initiator tRNA) migrates downstream until it recognises the start codon (Kozak, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about translation initiation, supported by a citation.

claims.evidence: This is the prevailing expectation in the field, which the authors' data challenge.

claims.source: Possibly, in the absence of UPF1 function, mRNPs acquire or retain native conformations that hinder their release from the chromosome and make them prone to aggregation and, consequently, cause nuclear retention.

claims.claim: A global role of UPF1 in mRNA release and export could explain why this protein is universally conserved in eukaryotes.
claims.source: Such a global role of UPF1 could explain, better than its involvement in NMD, why this protein is universally conserved in eukaryotes, why its depletion affects the expression of a large fraction of the genome, and possibly why expression of human UPF1 in rat models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) overcomes the pathology caused by over-expression or mutation of the RNA-binding protein TDP-43 (Barmada et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2015).

results.result: Three monoclonal antibodies targeting Drosophila UPF1 were generated and validated. Each antibody detected UPF1 as a single band by western blotting with minimal cross-reactivity, detected UPF1-GFP in transfected cells, and showed specific reduction upon UPF1-RNAi treatment. All three antibodies produced similar immunostaining patterns on polytene chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35, C38-C39, and C62-C64 collectively demonstrate antibody specificity through multiple independent validation approaches: western blotting showing single bands at expected molecular weights, detection of overexpressed UPF1-GFP, RNAi-mediated signal reduction, and consistent staining patterns across three different antibodies. These converging lines of evidence strongly support antibody specificity.

results.result: UPF1 is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm with a smaller fraction in the nucleus across multiple Drosophila tissues. Cell fractionation showed most UPF1 in the cytoplasmic fraction, and immunofluorescence revealed cytoplasmic and perinuclear localization with less intense nuclear staining in salivary glands and other larval tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C36-C37, and C40-C42 are supported by complementary biochemical (cell fractionation) and microscopy (immunofluorescence) data across multiple tissue types. The consistency between fractionation and imaging data, along with observations in multiple tissues, provides strong support for the subcellular distribution pattern.

results.result: UPF1 co-localizes with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) at the nuclear periphery in salivary glands. WGA is a lectin that predominantly interacts with O-GlcNAc-modified nuclear pore proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by co-localization imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and C44 is established knowledge supported by citation. The co-localization with WGA suggests UPF1 association with nuclear pores, consistent with nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling.

results.result: UPF1 is highly mobile within cells and shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm. FLIP experiments showed that photobleaching cytoplasmic UPF1 led to gradual depletion of nuclear UPF1, and FRAP experiments demonstrated rapid repopulation of bleached areas with halftimes of only a few seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by quantitative FLIP and FRAP data (Figure 1E-F) showing dynamic UPF1 mobility. The FLIP data demonstrate nuclear export (C47), while FRAP data show rapid mobility in both compartments (C48). The experimental design includes appropriate controls (neighboring cells), and the data are quantified with error bars.

results.result: UPF1 constantly shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm via a CRM1-dependent mechanism that requires its RNA helicase activity. LMB treatment caused rapid nuclear accumulation of wild-type UPF1 within 5-6 minutes, but the helicase-dead DE617AA mutant did not relocalize in response to LMB.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C51-C54, C57-C59, and C121 are strongly supported by live-cell imaging and LMB treatment experiments (Figures 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The key evidence is that wild-type UPF1 accumulates in the nucleus upon LMB treatment while the DE617AA mutant does not, directly demonstrating that helicase activity is required for shuttling. The time-course data show rapid kinetics. However, the mechanism is inferred to be CRM1-dependent based on LMB's known specificity rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: UPF1 associates with transcriptionally active regions on polytene chromosomes. UPF1 was predominantly found at interbands and puffs (transcriptionally active sites), co-localized with Ser2 Pol II, and redistributed to heat-shock puffs upon heat shock. UPF1 was recruited to both intron-containing and intronless activated genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61, C65-C66, and C68-C71 are supported by immunofluorescence microscopy on polytene chromosomes (Figures 3A-C). The heat-shock experiments provide functional evidence that UPF1 association depends on transcription (C66), and the ecdysone-inducible transgene experiment (C70-C71) provides an independent validation. Co-localization with Ser2 Pol II (C65) supports association with active transcription.

results.result: UPF1 associates genome-wide with nascent RNAs at most active Pol II transcription sites. ChIP-seq analysis showed UPF1 enrichment closely followed Ser2 Pol II profiles, with greatest enrichment at highly expressed genes. UPF1 was associated throughout gene bodies, typically downstream of the TSS-proximal Ser2 Pol II peak. Strong correlation was observed between UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II signals and between UPF1 and mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C72-C74, and C76-C83 are strongly supported by genome-wide ChIP-seq data (Figure 4) with multiple validations: correspondence between ChIP-seq and polytene immunostaining (C73-C74), ChIP-qPCR validation at specific genes, UPF1-RNAi controls showing reduced enrichment (C80), and metagene analyses (C81-C83). The correlation analyses (C78-C79) are quantitative and shown in scatter plots. The data are comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: UPF1 associates with some Pol III-transcribed genes, specifically 7SK and 7SL snRNA genes, but not with the more numerous tRNA genes. ChIP-seq data revealed selective UPF1 binding to specific Pol III genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C75, C91-C92 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C) showing UPF1 enrichment at 7SK and 7SL genes but not at tRNA genes. This selectivity is interesting but the mechanism is not explored. The data are clear but represent a minor observation in the context of the overall study.

results.result: UPF1 association with transcription sites depends on transcription elongation and nascent RNA. UPF1 did not associate with paused genes lacking elongation. UPF1 association was partially sensitive to RNase treatment (less so than hnRNPA1) and was reduced by DRB treatment that blocks transcription elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: ChIP-seq showing no UPF1 at paused-only genes (C84-C85), RNase sensitivity experiments on chromosomes and by ChIP (C86-C87), co-IP with Ser2 Pol II showing RNase sensitivity (C88), and DRB treatment reducing UPF1 association (C89-C90). The RNase sensitivity being intermediate between hnRNPA1 and eIF4AIII suggests both RNA-dependent and RNA-independent interactions.

results.result: Intron recognition interferes with UPF1 association with nascent pre-mRNAs. While UPF1 was recruited to both intron-containing and intronless genes, within intron-containing genes UPF1 showed significantly higher enrichment in exons compared to introns (p<0.001). This exon bias was genome-wide, confirmed by ChIP-qPCR, and was abolished by U1-70K depletion but persisted after depletion of EJC components. Genes with prominent exon-biased enrichment were efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C93-C101, C103-C105 are strongly supported by comprehensive ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 5). The genome-wide analysis (C98-C99) includes statistical testing with significant p-values. The U1-70K depletion experiment (C100) provides mechanistic insight supporting Model 2 (that splice site recognition blocks UPF1). The correlation with co-transcriptional splicing efficiency (C103-C104) adds functional context. This is a novel and well-supported finding.

results.result: UPF1 depletion causes defects in mRNA release from transcription sites and nuclear export. UPF1-depleted cells showed nuclear accumulation of poly(A) RNA, including large clusters in inter-chromosomal spaces and around nucleoli, and reduced cytoplasmic poly(A). On polytene chromosomes, UPF1 depletion dramatically increased the number and intensity of poly(A) signals at transcription sites, particularly at genes where UPF1 normally associates strongly (e.g., Actin5C at 5C). Expression of human UPF1 rescued this phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C106-C110, C112-C120, and C152-C154 are strongly supported by oligo(dT) FISH experiments (Figure 6) in both whole salivary glands and on polytene chromosomes. The rescue by human UPF1 expression (C109-C110, C112) demonstrates specificity. The correlation between UPF1 association and poly(A) accumulation upon depletion (C154) is compelling. This is a major novel finding revealing an unexpected nuclear role for UPF1.

results.result: The authors propose that UPF1's typical subcellular distribution (more cytoplasmic than nuclear) results from its association with abundant RNA cargos being continuously exported from the nucleus. They suggest UPF1 might bind SRP based on association with 7SL RNA genes, but may not bind ribosomal subunits based on exclusion from the nucleolus center.
results.evaluation: Claims C123, C126, and C128 represent speculative interpretations. C123 is a proposed model without direct experimental support. C126 is an inference from ChIP-seq data showing 7SL association, but direct binding to SRP is not demonstrated. C128 is inferred from immunofluorescence patterns but is not directly tested. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack definitive experimental validation.

results.result: The authors propose several mechanistic models and speculations about UPF1 function: that splicing might enhance UPF1 binding to downstream exons (Model 1) but is not necessary for loading; that UPF1 associates with all Pol II transcripts but splice site recognition interferes with intron binding (Model 2); that UPF1 scanning may influence splice site recognition; that the m7G cap might dictate UPF1 association; that UPF1 scanning is fast and discontinuous; and that reduced 5'UTR association might indicate translation-dependent binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131, C133, C136, C139-C142, C145-C146, and C149 are largely speculative interpretations and proposed models. While some are supported by correlative data (e.g., C140-C142 from FRAP/FLIP and ChIP patterns), most lack direct experimental validation. The m7G cap hypothesis (C136) is reasonable but untested. The translation-dependence speculation (C149) is based on correlative 5'UTR depletion data. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work but are not definitively supported.

results.result: The authors conclude that UPF1 plays an important genome-wide role in mRNA release from transcription sites and nuclear export in Drosophila. They speculate this could explain UPF1's universal conservation better than its NMD role, and suggest that in UPF1's absence, mRNPs may acquire conformations hindering chromosome release and promoting aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claim C156 is well-supported by the cumulative data showing poly(A) retention at transcription sites and nuclear accumulation upon UPF1 depletion (Figure 6). However, C157-C158 are more speculative interpretations about mechanism and evolutionary significance. The core conclusion (C156) about UPF1's role in mRNA release and export is strongly supported, but the mechanistic explanation (C157) and broader implications (C158) are inferences.

results.result: Background knowledge and literature context about UPF1, NMD, and related processes. These claims establish the field's understanding of UPF1 as an RNA helicase required for NMD, its biochemical properties, previous observations of nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling, and various proposed roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C24, C26-C31, C49-C50, C67, C102, C124-C125, C127, C137-C138, C143-C144, C148, C150-C151, C155, and C159 represent established knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the current study and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: No poly(A) accumulation was observed in UPF31 mutant glands or following RNAi depletion of EJC components Y14 or MAGO.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is stated as unpublished data without any figures or detailed description. While this control is important for demonstrating specificity to UPF1 (vs. general NMD factors), the lack of presented data makes it impossible to evaluate the quality or extent of these experiments.

results.result: The authors speculate that poly(A) accumulation at site 2C in wild-type cells may result from lack of UPF1 at this transcription site.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is a reasonable speculation based on the observation that 2C shows poly(A) accumulation in wild-type but no UPF1 association (C113-C114). This correlation supports the hypothesis, though it is not directly tested. The speculation is logical given the overall model.

results.result: The authors argue that simple RNA affinity is not the primary determinant of UPF1 association with nascent transcripts, based on observations that UPF1 does not associate with all highly transcribed genes and shows differential affinity for exons vs. introns. They also observe less UPF1 associated with 5' proximal regions/5'UTRs of some transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C135 and C147 are supported by the ChIP-seq data showing selective association patterns: UPF1 does not bind all Pol II genes (e.g., snRNAs), does not bind Pol I or most Pol III genes, shows exon bias within transcripts, and shows reduced 5' association at some genes. These observations collectively argue against simple sequence-independent RNA binding affinity as the sole determinant.
